perf.summary: O(k) walk can be reduced to O(n) by exploiting eventual periodicity of a functional graph (rho structure), since n is available.
perf.currentCost: for (long i = 0; i < k; i++) curr = f[curr]; performs exactly k dependent pointer chases. k is a long, so for large k this is unbounded work even though the trajectory from u repeats with period <= n. Each iteration is a serial cache-miss-prone dependent load.
perf.proposedChange: First walk at most n steps; detect entry of the cycle and its length L (e.g. via Floyd / Brent or tortoise-hare reusing FunctionalGraphCycleEntry). Let mu be the tail length (steps until cycle). If k <= mu, just walk k steps. Otherwise walk mu steps to the cycle entry, then take ((k - mu) % L) more steps. Total work O(mu + L) = O(n) instead of O(k).
perf.rationale: Trajectories in a functional graph are eventually periodic with period L <= n. Reducing k modulo L collapses arbitrarily large k to at most n + n steps, an asymptotic improvement from O(k) to O(n) whenever k > n.
perf.risk: Changes the performance model, not the result; output is identical for all valid k. Net loss when k < ~2n (the cycle-detection overhead dominates), so guard with: if (k <= n) use the simple loop, else use the rho-reduction. % on (k - mu): k>=mu and L>0 guarantee non-negative operands, so no signed-% surprise. Requires f to define a valid successor for every visited index (already assumed by unchecked Run).

perf.currentCost: n is passed but unused in the current O(k) implementation; it costs an argument slot and signals an unenforced contract.
perf.proposedChange: If the rho-reduction above is NOT adopted, n is dead and could be dropped. If the reduction IS adopted, n becomes load-bearing (bounds the detection walk) and should stay. Decide together with the complexity change.
perf.rationale: Either remove dead arg for a leaner call, or give it a real use via the periodicity optimization.
perf.risk: Dropping it breaks family signature uniformity; see CycleEntry note. No behavior change.
